title: Sorting with complete networks of stacks
contribution: First algorithmic treatment of sorting with a complete network of k stacks using the fewest shuffles: O(n^{1-ε}) inapproximability for k ≥ 4 via MIN k-PARTITION on circle graphs (itself O(n^{2-ε})-inapproximable), an O(n)-approximation with αk+1 stacks, and PSPACE-completeness of sortability under stacking constraints for every fixed k ≥ 3.
problem_entry: Knuth, Tarjan and Even-Itai characterized sortable permutations; with a cycle every permutation is sortable, so the open question is the minimum number of shuffles, which rail-yard, depot, parking and stowage applications pose but had studied only as parallel-stack sortability (abstract; pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Stack choice as a colour in the permutation's circle graph: proper k-colourings are shuffle-free sortings and monochromatic edges bound shuffles from both sides (γ ≤ (n-1)L, L ≤ 2γ), although fewest monochromatic edges is not fewest shuffles (Fig. 1); merge sort and a phase algorithm on an approximate colouring give the positive results (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Not a MILP: directed network with source and sink, k ≥ 2 stack nodes on s-t paths, at least one cycle; complete networks for the hardness and approximation results; unbounded stack heights; Thm 4 adds a conflict digraph on items for fixed k ≥ 3 without the initial configuration, height bounds or k-as-input of the earlier proof (pp. 3-4, 9).
proof_devices: gap amplification: each chord replaced by s = n^{2/ε-1} parallel chords and all copies recoloured after the least-conflicting one, so an optimal k-colouring has 0 or at least s^2 = N^{2-ε} monochromatic edges (Thm 1, pp. 5-6)
charging: each shuffle pays for at most n-1 monochromatic edges (Lemma 1, p. 6)
phase construction with shuffle-and-reverse giving 2γ shuffles from a colouring (Lemma 2, p. 6)
one forced shuffle per phase of the αk+1-stack algorithm, so L* ≥ p and 3n·L* shuffles (Thm 3, pp. 7-8)
Remark 1: a linear guarantee is needed only on instances with o(log n) optimal shuffles, merge sort covers the rest (p. 7)
reduction from Nondeterministic Constraint Logic with OR/AND gadgets on two stacks per node, compressed to three stacks; full proof deferred to a full version (Thm 4, pp. 9-11)
limits_future: Tightness of the positive results against the hardness bound called unsatisfactory; augmentation best possible only for this algorithm; Thm 4 proved only in a promised full version; open: k = 2 and 3, the logarithmic gap, a lower bound on shuffles other than circle-graph colouring, queues and the midnight constraint (pp. 2, 7-8, 10-11).

method_links.note: Step 6 carried into a theory paper: the positive results come with their gap to the lower bound and the reason no better bound is in reach (circle-graph colouring is the only handle, clique-based bounds cannot beat log ω); no computation, so steps 1-5 do not apply.
Step 5 (publish what stays open) in a research paper rather than a synthesis: the paper ends on open problems, among them an alternative lower bound on shuffles it cannot supply.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: hardness result as licence for the method
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The conclusion reads the hardness results as explaining the lack of elegant and efficient algorithms; the same move in S051 (p. 10) and D002 (p. 3).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization version of a characterization problem
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Enters where the literature characterized feasibility (sortability) and asks for the minimum-shuffle version that applications need; the same entry in S051 (p. 2).

transferable: To turn the NP-hardness of deciding whether the optimum is 0 into inapproximability, blow each element up into s copies so that any nonzero optimum jumps to at least s^2, choosing s so that the gap is N^{2-ε} in the new size (Thm 1, pp. 5-6).

When reducing to a known problem whose objective is only related to yours, show a one-instance counterexample to equivalence (Fig. 1, p. 4) and prove two-sided bounds instead (γ ≤ (n-1)L and L ≤ 2γ, p. 6).
If a simple algorithm already guarantees O(n log n), a linear guarantee is needed only on instances whose optimum is o(log n); return the better of the two solutions (Remark 1, p. 7).

quotes.text: It is surprising however, that theory avoided the apparent need for shuffles—only sortability, not sorting itself has been considered so far.
Even though their tightness w.r.t. our hardness result is unsatisfactory, we will discuss that they are the best we may currently hope for.

title: On minimum k-modal partitions of permutations
contribution: NP-hardness of partitioning a permutation into the fewest k-modal (and unimodec) subsequences, the first MIP formulations for provably optimal partitions (a compact network-design model and its Dantzig-Wolfe set-partitioning version with equal LP bound), LP-rounding approximations (factors 2, 3, k+1, 2(k+1)), an Ω(log n) online lower bound and a computational comparison on random permutations.
problem_entry: Minimum monotone partition is NP-hard; the structural literature (Erdős-Szekeres, Chung, Steele) bounds subsequence lengths, while shunting-yard and tram-depot track assignment needs optimum partitions computed (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Decreasing subsequences as s-t paths in a split permutation graph (min-cost flow solves DECREASING); k+1 chained components with binary lower-bound selectors give a network-design MIP for k-MODAL, whose Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation is the set-partitioning model with integral shortest-path pricing and hence the same LP bound; LP rounding of the compact model yields the approximations (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: Permutations of {1,...,n}, fixed k; network-design MIP with continuous flows and binary selectors; the rounding theorem needs generalized bound constraints with at most ρ ≥ 2 variables and ρ·P ⊆ P (flows without upper bounds); the construction relies on transitivity of the order, so not posets (pp. 3, 5-8, 11).
proof_devices: NP-hardness by reduction from restricted MONOTONE (ℓ increasing, m decreasing lines) with block gadgets A_h, B_h and an induction claim on covering lines (Thm 1, pp. 3-5)
LP bounds of compact and set-partitioning models coincide because pricing (shortest path in an acyclic network) is always integral (Lemma 2, p. 7)
ρ-approximation: round selectors up to a representative with y ≥ 1/ρ, re-solve the then integral flow LP; ρ·x_LP stays feasible since ρ·P ⊆ P (Thm 4, p. 8)
integrality gap at least 3/2 shown by [6,2,1,4,3,5] with LP 2.0 and IP 3.0 (p. 8)
online lower bound Ω(log n) by an adversary that halves the remaining value range (Thm 6, p. 9)
tight n/4 examples for Next Fit and Best Fit (Lemmas 7-8, pp. 9-10)
experiments: Random permutations (Knuth shuffle), n = 30, 60, 90, 120, 100 instances per size, CPLEX 9.0 default, 900 CPU s, Athlon MP 2800+; average and worst-case ratios to the optimum for greedy, LP rounding, LP bound and online rules; flow MIP averages 218-255 s at n = 120 while the fully generated set-partitioning IP almost always times out from n = 90 or 120 (p. 10; Table 1, p. 11).
limits_future: Set-partitioning model enumerated, not priced, and a true branch-and-price code would probably win on larger instances; bounded track length makes pricing an NP-hard resource-constrained shortest path; open: PTAS, beating 1.71 with LP techniques, an online algorithm matching Ω(log n), look-ahead, posets (pp. 10-11).

method_links.note: Steps 1-2 and the stop rule: the compact network-design model comes first, the set-partitioning model is derived from it by Dantzig-Wolfe, the bound gain is zero because pricing has the integrality property, and the compact MIP in CPLEX is far faster than the enumerated set-partitioning IP; the extended model is kept only for flexibility with 'dirty' side constraints.
Step 6: worst cases next to averages, a 'conservative judgment' of the times, and the fairness remark that a real branch-and-price code would probably beat the compact MIP on larger instances.
Step 1 and taste B2: a single test set of random permutations sized by the application (90-120 elements for rail car shunting), no real or public instances and no second set.

LP rounding for choice constraints Σ_{j∈I_q} y_j = 1 over a scalable polyhedron (ρ·P ⊆ P): fix to 1 a representative with y_LP ≥ 1/ρ in each group and re-solve the integral flow LP; a ρ-approximation (Thm 4, pp. 7-8).
Give the smallest instance you know with a large integrality gap ([6,2,1,4,3,5]: LP 2.0, IP 3.0, p. 8).
In a heuristics table report average and worst-case ratio to the proven optimum per instance size and mark runs that hit the time limit (Table 1, p. 11).
coauthors: Gabriele Di Stefano, Stefan Krause, Uwe T. Zimmermann

quotes.text: Theoretical hardness legitimates studying and applying computationally expensive approaches like solving (probably large scale) mixed integer programs.
To be fair at this point we remark that a true branch-and-price algorithm would probably outmatch the network design MIP in terms of computation time on larger instances.

title: Third European Conference on combinatorics graph theory and applications-Preface
contribution: Guest editors' preface (Felsner, Lübbecke, Nešetřil) to the Discrete Mathematics special issue of selected EuroComb05 papers: programme committee, thematic grouping of twelve papers, invited talks and the 2005 European Prize in Combinatorics.
limits_future: Editorial service only: a volume completed close to one year after the Berlin conference of September 2005; nothing about the editors' own research (pp. 1-2).

quotes.text: Most of the papers we collected in this volume have a distinct algorithmic flavor, and all of them are connected to graph theory in its broadest sense.

title: Sequencing and Scheduling in Coil Coating with Shuttles
contribution: Exact model of integrated coil-coating planning with shuttle coaters, a 2-union-graph model of tank assignment and concurrent setup (strongly NP-hard, FPT in the number of coaters), a deployed genetic-algorithm heuristic for Salzgitter Flachstahl, and a branch-and-price lower bound on a combinatorial relaxation (valid under the FIFO tank rule) giving 4-15% gaps.
problem_entry: An industrial planning task: shuttle coaters turn coil sequencing into an integrated tank-assignment and concurrent-setup scheduling problem needed already to evaluate one sequence, which does not decompose and must be tackled in its entirety; presented as the first optimization work on coil coating (pp. 2-5, 7).
key_idea: For a fixed sequence, tank assignments with feasible setup schedules are weighted rectangles of a 2-union graph and an optimal pair is a maximum-weight independent set; the fast heuristic drops the coupling work resource and scales interval lengths by α to get MWIS on an interval graph inside a genetic algorithm; a block-concatenation relaxation solved by branch-and-price certifies it (pp. 9-24).
assumptions: Makespan objective; local setups by consecutive coils, global setups by the previous coil on the same tank; one non-preemptive concurrent-setup team with slowdown λ ≥ 1; FPT needs max p_i/(λ t_c) polynomially bounded (about one in data); the lower bound is valid only for an online tank rule that concatenates, so FIFO is assumed; confidential SZFG batches of 20-40 coils (pp. 5-8, 19, 21-23, 25).
proof_devices: strong NP-hardness of maximum independent set on diagonally k-partitionable 2-union graphs by a 3-SAT reduction (Thm 1, pp. 12-14)
dynamic program over states (coil, one rectangle per coater) as a longest path in the state DAG, O(n^2·N^{2k}) (pp. 17-18)
candidate-time-point lemma bounding the work-interval start times (Lemma 1, pp. 18-19)
'don't look back too far' relaxation: exact global cost only inside blocks of k = 4 coils, local cost between blocks (pp. 21-22, 26)
pricing by depth-first backtracking with a dual-based pruning rule, since a subsequence's cost is known only when complete (p. 23)
branching on original variables x_{p,j} by forbidding or enforcing coil j at position p in pricing, incompatible columns bounded to zero, penalized artificial columns (pp. 23-24)
restricted master seeded with subsequences of the GA's FIFO solution (p. 23)
experiments: Nine representative SZFG instances normalized to the GA makespan (confidential data); trivial, TSP and IP (k = 4) lower bounds with IP gap% 4.28-15.08; SZFG reference plans 1.06-1.35 times the GA makespan on six instances; one GA parameter set fixed by testing; no hardware, run times or time limits beyond the 180 s requirement (pp. 15, 25-26).
limits_future: Own tank-assignment heuristics and local search at best slightly beat the FIFO rule; the bound is improvable (not all IPs solved to integer optimality, only k = 4), although the conclusion says the IP is solved to optimality; future work only the hope that the ideas carry to similar applications (pp. 25-27).

method_links.note: Steps 5-6: branch-and-price on SCIP for the bounding IP, branching on the original assignment variables carried into pricing.
Decomposition used to certify a heuristic, not to solve the problem; no compact formulation of the relaxation reported as a yardstick.

Real planner data, the planners' own plans as baseline, and the authors' own tank-assignment ideas reported as no better than FIFO with the caveat that other data may differ. Also H2 evidence (the deployed GA certified by a branch-and-price lower bound, p. 21; conditional on FIFO, p. 22) and Workflow A step 4 / H3 evidence (planners' validation loop, FIFO requirement dropped after the savings were seen, pp. 20, 24-25).

Step 6: the headline 'within 5-15% of the optimum' (abstract, introduction, conclusion) drops the FIFO condition under which section 5 proves the bound; 'able to solve to optimality' (p. 27) against 'did not solve all instances to integer optimality' (p. 26); a self-praising conclusion of the kind taste B3 warns of.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strong NP-hardness of the tank-assignment and scheduling subproblem is offered to justify the heuristic approach; with S034 (p. 11) and S051 (p. 10).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The fast heuristic is the exact interval model with the coupling resource relaxed and lengths scaled by α; the text says the heuristics could not have been developed without the structural sections; compare S051 (pp. 7-8).

transferable: To certify a heuristic for sequencing with history-dependent costs, relax the history: cost blocks of k consecutive items exactly, charge only local cost between blocks, and solve the block-concatenation IP by branch-and-price (pp. 21-23).
State the condition under which a bound is valid (here an online tank rule that concatenates) wherever the gap is stated, the abstract included (p. 22 against p. 1).

Branch on an original assignment variable (item j at position p) inside pricing: remove j from p (down) or all other items from p (up), bound incompatible columns to zero, keep one penalized artificial column per covering row (pp. 23-24).
Seed the restricted master with columns cut from the heuristic's best solution (p. 23).

From an exact but slow model of the subproblem (MWIS with a shared resource) get a fast heuristic by dropping the shared resource and scaling interval lengths by a tuned factor α, best near 0.5 here (pp. 19, 25).
With confidential data, normalize every bound and the practitioners' plan to the heuristic's value and report gap% per instance (Table 3, p. 26).
coauthors: Wiebke Höhn, Felix G. König, Rolf H. Möhring

quotes.text: Assessing the quality of heuristic solutions is not only a theoretical contribution, but an important question in practice: How much optimization potential is left?

title: Frontmatter, Table of Contents, Preface, Organization
contribution: Front matter of the ATMOS'10 proceedings (OASIcs 14) edited with Thomas Erlebach: contents, a joint preface (30 submissions, at least three referees each, 12 accepted, invited paper by Caprara) and the programme committee he co-chaired from TU Darmstadt.
limits_future: Editorial service only; the call's stated interests (integration of planning stages, online or stochastic settings, heuristics for real-world instances) are a joint editorial text, nothing attributable to Lübbecke alone (pp. 7, 9).

quotes.text: Of particular interest were: the successful integration of several (sub)problems or planning stages, algorithms operating in an online/realtime or stochastic setting, and heuristic approaches (including approximation algorithms) for real-world instances.

title: A branch-and-price algorithm for multi-mode resource leveling
contribution: A shift-based branch-and-price algorithm on SCIP for multi-mode resource leveling with calendars (turnaround scheduling), with problem-specific branching, propagation and heuristics, solving instances with up to 50 multi-mode jobs and beating the time-indexed MIP in CPLEX 12 on the larger instances.
problem_entry: Turnaround scheduling from chemical engineering becomes resource leveling once the horizon is fixed; heuristics dominate because time-indexed MIPs have very weak LP relaxations and often fail already on 30 jobs, and an earlier column-generation bound lost to Lagrangian relaxation at 30 jobs (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Decompose the time horizon by the resource calendars: columns are sub-schedules of a working shift, one configuration per job in the master, start and completion times linked to configurations so their duals enter pricing; precedence stays in the master on original variables; per-shift pricing is an NP-hard leveling IP whose solution method is not stated (pp. 5-7).
assumptions: MPSm,∞|prec,shifts|Σ c_k max r_k: non-preemptive jobs, one resource each, several modes, renewable resources with availability periods, fixed horizon; self-generated instances (30/60, 50/70, 50/100 jobs/edges, 10 each, 3 modes, two resources, five calendars) because no public set has shifts (pp. 2-4, 9-10).
proof_devices: two-job example showing the time-indexed LP losing timing information and branching on x_{jt} misleading (Fig. 2, p. 5)
branching order R_k, then S_j, then C_j found by experiments, only where a configuration variable is fractional (p. 7)
edge-finding propagation adapted to multiple modes, also passing branching decisions to pricing (p. 7)
ready scheduling over all mode combinations of s = 6 jobs and a binary-search leveling heuristic, every feasible schedule added as columns (pp. 8-9)
SCIP 1.2.0.6 with custom plug-ins for pricer, branching and heuristics (p. 10)
experiments: 150 runs (30 instances × 5 calendars), 30 min limit; branch-and-price on Intel 2.66 GHz against the time-indexed MIP in CPLEX 12 with quad-core parallelization on a stronger machine, plus an ablation without the LP-solution and ready-scheduling heuristics on 30 jobs; mean time, number of best known lower and upper bounds, timeouts; by the timeout columns 118/150 (78.7%) solved by branch-and-price vs 64/150 (42.7%) by CPLEX (text: 80% vs 43%); CPLEX faster on C3 and ahead on C2 with 70 edges (pp. 10-12).
limits_future: The problem-specific heuristics barely change the number of instances solved; the summary states only the belief that 30-job instances remain hard and encouragement to continue (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Steps 2, 3, 5, 6: the compact time-indexed MIP in a current solver is the baseline; the column object (a shift sub-schedule) comes from the calendar structure named as the motivation; the code is a set of SCIP plug-ins; branching on original variables.
The stop rule's test (pricing more than a generic MIP) cannot be applied from the text: the pricing problem is an NP-hard leveling IP whose solution method is not stated.

A per-component ablation (branch-and-price without heuristics), the competitor's stronger machine flagged in the text as the checkpoint asks, the CPLEX wins visible in the tables. Also H2 evidence: the heuristic judged against branch-and-price bounds, 'from both ends' (p. 2), best upper bound in 68% of instances (p. 11).

Step 6: the claimed improvement over [MMS10] (p. 2) has no comparison in the computational section; 'significantly outperforms' without a test; 'the best results across all shift configurations' holds for upper bounds only, not for lower bounds, time and timeouts on C2 with 70 edges; the heuristics' average time gain hides a slowdown on C1; 78.7% reported as 80%.
Step 1 and taste B2: one self-generated factorial set modelled on PSPLib, justified by the absence of a public set with shifts; no second, general set.

transferable: When a time-indexed MIP is weak and resources have calendars, decompose the horizon by shifts: one column per sub-schedule of a shift, a one-configuration-per-job constraint, and start/completion linking equalities that feed time-dependent duals into pricing (pp. 5-6).

Branch on original variables in a fixed order (capacities, start times, completion times), only where an associated column variable is fractional, and propagate (edge-finding) so pricing sees the decisions (p. 7).
Add every feasible schedule a primal heuristic finds to the master as columns to cut pricing rounds (p. 9).
Report per instance class mean time, how often each code reaches the best known lower and upper bound, and timeouts, plus a column for the code with its heuristics off (Tables 1-2, pp. 10-11).

quotes.text: For the standard MIP (1)–(6) we used CPLEX 12 with quad-core parallelization on a stronger machine.
It achieves the best results across all shift configurations, in the worst case 88% of the best upper bounds are found.

title: Nested Column Generation applied to the Crude Oil Tanker Routing and Scheduling Problem with Split Pickup and Split Delivery
contribution: A three-level nested column generation (all-ship master, per-ship branch-and-price over routes and cargo patterns, ESPPTW route generation) on SCIP for crude oil tanker routing with split pickup and split delivery, run as a heuristic on twelve realistic instances, with slightly better schedules than earlier column-pregeneration codes except on the two largest.
problem_entry: A rich maritime problem (heterogeneous fleet, many grades, many-to-many relations, arc capacities, quantity-dependent service times) where exact split-delivery VRP methods exist but rely on at most one split customer per route, which fails for split pickup and split delivery; claimed as a general exact methodology for such problems (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Decouple routing from service: since two split locations, several commodities and arc capacities destroy label dominance and make reduced costs non-local, routes come from labelling and quantities from column generation over extreme cargo patterns, nested inside a per-ship branch-and-price below an all-ship master; exact in principle, used as a heuristic (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Level 1: binary route variables, continuous pattern weights, integer count of unused ships; level 2: a MIP with a big-M timing constraint; deterministic sailing times, one visit per time window and ship, approximate waiting limits that may cut optimal routes, at most two voyages per route; twelve reality-related instances with 2-15 ships (pp. 2, 4-6, 9-10).
proof_devices: route variables substituted out of convexity and visit constraints so that a new route adds no row (p. 4)
branching on original arc and node flows per ship at both master levels with SCIP's built-in branching (pp. 6-7)
time-boxed inner pricing (first column below c_lim = -1 or t_lim = 60 s) with a ship queue that re-examines timed-out ships without the limit (pp. 7-8, 10)
greedy cargo-pattern generator (at most 30 patterns per voyage), extreme patterns only if it fails (pp. 9-10)
heuristic label dominance on cost and time first, exact dominance when it yields no column (p. 9)
presolve, cuts and propagation disabled during branch-and-price to keep the dual bound correct (p. 10)
final price-and-branch run in CPLEX on the master with all generated columns (p. 10)
experiments: SCIP 1.1.0.6 with CPLEX 11.2, Core 2 Duo 3 GHz, 6 GB, one core, two runs per machine, 12 h then a CPLEX run; optimality proven for 3 of 12 instances, root gaps 0.4-6.6% where available, no valid bound for instances 8-12, level 2 takes 96-100% of the time; up to 8% and 1-7% better than two column-pregeneration codes, not on the two largest instances, costs not directly comparable (pp. 10-12).
limits_future: Tail-off and long LP times at level 2, memory limits in the final run, a primal heuristic too weak to replace the second run; future: parallel level-2 solves, better pattern generation, branching on column sets, valid inequalities, tailored primal heuristics, exact fast cargo-pattern generation, a generic view of the problem class (pp. 12-13).

method_links.note: Steps 5-6: SCIP chosen for its tree management and plug-in support 'for a proof-of-concept'; branching on original arc and node variables at both levels.
Steps 2 and 4 absent: no compact model run as a yardstick and no probe; the decomposition is chosen from the argued failure of label dominance and compared with column-pregeneration codes.

Step 6 in the body: optimality claimed only for instances 1, 2 and 4, no gaps where no valid bound exists, 'a general conclusion should not be drawn', the two largest instances not improved, costs marked not directly comparable. Also H1 evidence: partial and heuristic pricing because of tail-off, heuristic dominance and patterns before exact ones (pp. 7, 9).
The abstract says the schedules improve on previous studies without the exception of the two largest instances; competitors not re-run under identical conditions (step 3) and runs share machines.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: split a pricing level when label dominance fails
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Routes by labelling, quantities by column generation over the extreme points of the per-route quantity polyhedron, nested inside the per-ship pricing; the conclusion presents it as avoiding a possibly extremely difficult dynamic program.

transferable: If quantities make reduced costs non-local and kill label dominance, keep labelling for routes only and generate quantity patterns as extreme points of a per-route polyhedron by column generation, convex-combined in the master (pp. 3-5).
Substitute route variables out of convexity and visit constraints so that the master does not grow by a row per new route (p. 4).
Time-box inner pricing (first column below a threshold or t seconds) and re-examine timed-out subproblems without the limit before declaring the LP optimal (pp. 7-8).
Check which framework features would invalidate a column-generation dual bound (presolve, cuts, propagation) and switch them off during pricing (p. 10).
Close with price-and-branch: solve the final master with all generated columns as a MIP in a commercial solver (p. 10).

quotes.text: It should be noted that the approach is exact in principle, even though we will use it as a heuristic.
During branch-and-price we have to disable SCIP's preprocessing, cut generation, and propagation functionalities to ensure a correct dual bound.

title: Automatic Decomposition and Branch-and-Price—A Status Report
contribution: Sole-authored status report on automating Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation and branch-and-price: why generic codes still need expert input, hypergraph-based detection of bordered block-diagonal structure, GCG's features on SCIP, and success criteria and open questions for the project; no computational results in the written text.
problem_entry: An adoption gap: Dantzig-Wolfe, column generation and branch-and-price are well understood but not out-of-the-box usable by everyday OR practitioners, because generic codes (BaPCod, DIP, G12) need a user-specified decomposition and own codes restart with each application; the interest dates from collecting material for the 2005 primer (p. 5).
key_idea: Detect a decomposable structure in the flat matrix and feed it to a generic branch-and-price solver that keeps both formulations; the opening derives bin-packing pattern and aggregated set-partitioning models from the compact model, noting the loss of unique reconstruction (pp. 1-7).
assumptions: IPs min{c^T x : Ax ≥ b, Dx ≥ d, x ∈ Z^n_+} with D block-diagonal (bordered block-diagonal matrix), X assumed bounded 'but this is no restriction'; LP file plus optional decomposition file; only 10teams shown (pp. 3-4, 6).
proof_devices: row-column hypergraph of the nonzeros: connected components are blocks; removing a minimum set of row hyperedges reveals a bordered block-diagonal form (NP-hard, heuristics, several small k tried) (pp. 5-6)
hypergraph clustering being tried to avoid fixing the number of blocks (p. 6)

GCG: best-guess reformulation, convexification or discretization, aggregation of identical blocks, both formulations kept for branching and separation on original variables, Ryan-Foster branching, generic primal heuristics, SCIP pseudo-costs, presolving and propagation (pp. 6-7)
experiments: none in the text: the abstract promises computational results, the experiments are reported in the talk, and only one detected structure (10teams, Fig. 1) is shown (pp. 1, 5-6).
positioning: Vanderbeck's generic branching and BaPCod as inspiration, DIP and G12 as other generic codes, all requiring a user-specified decomposition; the IPCO 2011 experiments on general MIPs as the first step (p. 5).
writing: Tutorial opening on bin packing; four reader types with their pain points before the argument, closed by 'Read on'; personal motivation in the plural; hedged detection results; a discussion that states goal and open problem instead of summarising; 'we' for the project, 'I' only in the acknowledgments (pp. 1-7).
limits_future: Goals as success criteria: no win expected over branch-and-cut on the average instance, anything but a win on structured instances would be a failure, so reliable detection (or concluding none) is the challenge; open: detection tailored to the sparse degree-2 hypergraph, clustering instead of fixed k, a theory of what makes a good structure and how to set up a good IP model (pp. 6-7).

method_links.note: Steps 1 and 6: the compact original formulation first, column models derived from it; GCG keeps both formulations so branching and cutting work on original variables; branch-and-cut as the yardstick.

Dating of the increment: in 2012 his sole voice frames the generic solver as needing no user input or expert knowledge and useful to a non-expert, the framing SKILL.md says was overturned after 2017; yet one of the four reader types is already the one who does not know whether a hand-built branch-and-price code is worth the time and considerable effort, the seed of step 4's probe.

Steps 1 and 6: the test target moved from general MIPs (a proof of concept) to instances that bear structure, and the success criterion is fixed before any result (no win on the average instance, a win on structured ones required).
The abstract promises computational results that the written text does not contain.

transferable: Introduce a decomposition by deriving it from the compact model step by step (assignment model, per-bin patterns, aggregated patterns) and say what each step loses (symmetry, unique reconstruction) (pp. 1-3).
Detect bordered block-diagonal structure with the row-column hypergraph of the nonzeros: delete a minimum set of row hyperedges to split it into k components and try several small k (pp. 5-6).
Write down the success criterion of a generic method before testing: what it need not beat (branch-and-cut on the average instance) and what it must beat (structured instances) (p. 7).
Open an expository paper with a short list of reader types and the question each brings (p. 4).
